nameStory: This sea cucumber doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists just call it by its scientific name Chiridota laevis. The genus name 'Chiridota' comes from Greek meaning 'little hand,' referring to the tiny hand-like feeding tentacles around its mouth. The species name 'laevis' means 'smooth' in Latin, describing its sleek, polished appearance.
description: Chiridota laevis is a small, worm-like sea cucumber that lives buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms along New England's coast. This marine animal looks like a translucent, pinkish or whitish sausage, typically growing 2-4 inches long and about as thick as a pencil. Unlike the spiky sea cucumbers you might see in tide pools, this species has a completely smooth, almost glass-like body. It belongs to a group called sea cucumbers, which are actually relatives of sea stars and sea urchins, not vegetables at all!

idTips.label: Smooth, translucent body
idTips.description: The body feels slippery and smooth like wet glass, with a translucent quality that lets you see internal structures as dark shadows

idTips.label: Worm-like shape
idTips.description: Elongated and cylindrical like a small earthworm, but much more delicate and squishy to the touch

idTips.label: Feeding tentacles
idTips.description: Tiny, finger-like projections around the mouth end that feel like soft, wet threads when gently touched

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: Usually 2-4 inches long, pencil-thick, with a pinkish-white or clear coloration that may have a slight iridescent sheen

idTips.label: Contractile movement
idTips.description: When disturbed, it quickly contracts into a shorter, fatter shape, feeling firm and tense rather than limp

habitat: Found in subtidal sandy and muddy bottoms from shallow waters down to about 150 feet deep along New England's Atlantic coast. You're most likely to encounter one when digging for clams or examining dredged material, as they live buried several inches below the sediment surface. They prefer areas with fine sediment where they can easily burrow and filter-feed on organic particles.

seasonality.spring: May be encountered when clam digging begins in warmer waters. Look for them in dredged material or when digging deep in sandy flats.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when water temperatures are warmest. Occasionally found by beachcombers examining storm-washed sediments or in marine biology collections.
seasonality.fall: Still active but moving deeper as water temperatures drop. Less likely to be encountered by casual observers.
seasonality.winter: Remain buried deep in sediment, rarely encountered except by researchers or deep clam digging in protected areas.

funFact: When threatened, Chiridota laevis can actually break off and regenerate its tail end as a distraction technique, just like some lizards do - except this one lives underwater and can regrow the missing parts within a few months!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small marine worms, but unlike true worms, sea cucumbers have a distinct mouth end with tiny tentacles and feel much more delicate and squishy. Remember: if it looks like a translucent sausage with tiny fingers on one end, it's probably this sea cucumber, not a worm.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'sea cucumber,' this animal is not a plant at all but an echinoderm - the same group that includes starfish and sea urchins. The cucumber name comes from their general shape, but they're 100% animal and are actually important recyclers of ocean sediments.
compareHints: **Note: Limited observation data (only 2 records) means identification details may be incomplete.** As the only Chiridota species commonly found in New England waters, it's most similar to other burrowing sea cucumbers in the region, but differs by having a completely smooth body without the bumps, spines, or tough skin found on most other local sea cucumber species. Its translucent, delicate appearance makes it quite distinctive once you know what to look for.
